title: Deathless
summary: The series’ final part, titled ‘Deathless’, argues from Romans 5:12–17 that sin and death came through Adam but righteousness and life come through Jesus, the ‘last Adam’, a wholly new kind of humanity in whom believers are already placed. The preacher contends that the gospel Jesus preached is about victory on this side of death: ‘death’ in Scripture means decay — anything not keeping pace with an ever-increasing kingdom — not hell or eternal separation, and the popular afterlife-centred gospel is attributed to Platonic philosophy rather than to Jesus. Using John 11, Heb 2:14–15 and John 10, he teaches that Christ released believers from the fear of death and its bondage, that ‘saved’ (sōzō) means wholeness now, and that the ‘thief’ is anyone offering life by earning. He closes with three keys to life over decay — choose, confess and know — calling the local church to bring life to its city, and prays for healing, financial increase and generosity.
thesis: Because Jesus, the last Adam, has conquered death, the true gospel is a ‘deathless’ one in which believers reign in life now, free from decay and the fear of death, rather than a message whose hope begins only after death.

flow.step: The church is the hope of the world
flow.text: Creation waits for the manifestation of the sons of God, not for a rapture or death; Jesus sat down because His work is finished, so the local ekklēsia must now govern and bring life to its city.

Adam was a created living soul, an image and a ‘vacuum’; Jesus is the begotten, life-giving Spirit and a ‘resource’. Believers are not restored to Adam but placed in Christ as the church of the firstborn.

flow.step: Sin and death vs righteousness and life
flow.text: Rom 5:12 traces sin and death to Adam; since neither is found in the new Man, the solution is righteousness and life.

flow.step: Salvation on this side of death
flow.text: Jesus never used fear of the afterlife as motivation; His gospel gives victory now. The afterlife is a component of the gospel, not the gospel, and believers ‘sleep’ when they leave the body.

flow.step: Soul is not eternal; Platonic gospel
flow.text: The soul (mind, will, emotions) dies with the body while the spirit is eternal; the idea of a punished immortal soul is attributed to Socrates and Plato as a tool of social control, not to Jesus.
Those who receive abundant grace and the gift of righteousness reign in life; the gospel is a ‘live-abundantly-now pass’, removing decay from every area of life.
Biblical death is said never to mean hell or eternal separation but universal decay; expecting to decline ‘over the hill’ and be saved by dying is an odd gospel.

Jesus is the resurrection for those who die and the life for those who live and believe, who ‘shall never die’; heirs do not need to die to inherit. Jesus even kept His finances free of decay, as the feeding of the 5,000 shows.
Christ became human to destroy the devil’s power of death and free those enslaved by fear of death; bodily death is only the ‘recognition point’ of a life lived under decay.

flow.step: Saved means whole; the thief is legalism
flow.text: Sōzō means healed, delivered, made whole, kept safe; in John 10 the thieves are those who offer life by earning, while Jesus gives abundant life.
Life over decay depends on choosing life (Deut 30), confessing it (Prov 18:21) and knowing truth (Hos 4:6), abandoning doctrines of death.

The church ceased to be Adamic 2,000 years ago; Christ’s victory over death is in believers’ past. The preacher calls for repentance from a lifestyle of death and prays for healing, provision and generosity.

teachings.title: A gospel that changes cities
teachings.body: The preacher states directly what he had previously said in passing, aiming to lay a foundation for a gospel that will actually transform the city.

teachings.title: The local church is the hope of the world
teachings.body: Creation is waiting for the manifestation of the sons of God — not for a rapture, death or Jesus’ coming — so that it may enter their liberty. Believers are therefore the hope of the world.

teachings.title: God sits down when He is finished
teachings.body: God rested on the seventh day because creation was finished; likewise Jesus ascended above every principality and power and sat at the Father’s right hand, meaning His work is done and the church is ‘tagged in’.

teachings.title: Return to the local body
teachings.body: Being a functioning member of a local ekklēsia, the institution meant to govern human life, must be reprioritised. Local viewers watching online are called back to attend in person because they have function and destiny.

teachings.title: Adam was not the goal
teachings.body: Paul’s contrast is not between fallen Adam and risen Jesus but between two kinds of men: Adam was created in God’s image and was flawed from the beginning, while Jesus was begotten, the unique (‘monogenetic’) Son. A gospel that restores us to Adam restores us to an image with Adam’s shortcomings; Jesus is a better Adam.

teachings.title: Living soul vs life-giving spirit
teachings.body: Adam became a living soul — a vacuum needing input — while Jesus, the last Adam, is a life-giving spirit — a resource. Since He is the last Adam, there are no more vacuums; believers are now suppliers from whom rivers of living water flow.

teachings.title: Church of the firstborn
teachings.body: Jesus is the firstborn among many brethren; believers did not come into being in sequence but all at once in Him, so collectively we are as He is, not as Adam was.

teachings.title: Sin and death came through one man
teachings.body: Rom 5:12 shows sin entered through Adam and death through sin, spreading to all. If Jesus is a never-before-seen humanity, sin and death cannot be found in Him, so the solution to sin and death is righteousness and life.

teachings.title: Salvation is on this side of death
teachings.body: The prophets and Jesus offer no message that gives hope only after death; Jesus never used fear of the afterlife to motivate discipleship. Mixing the two (‘mostly about heaven, a little about now’) is called a gross reduction of Christ’s accomplishment.

teachings.title: Problems are not solved by dying
teachings.body: Believers who hope that money troubles, pain, depression, anxiety or a bad marriage will end only at death are believing a false gospel of ‘die and your problems are over’.

teachings.title: The afterlife is a component, not the gospel
teachings.body: Something does happen when we leave the body: Jesus defeated death so it never has the final say, and believers are with the Lord. God gave a safeguard against death called sleep; but the afterlife is part of the gospel, not the gospel itself.

teachings.title: The soul is not an eternal entity
teachings.body: The soul is described as mind, will and emotions — the seat of affections and aversions — that animates the body and is what people see of us. It is a component of humanity that dies with the body; the spirit is the eternal component.

teachings.title: Salvation of the soul is the end of faith
teachings.body: 1 Peter says the salvation of the soul is the end of faith; the series reads this not as the soul’s eternal destination but as the point when, no believing being left to do, the soul is in perfect harmony with the spirit.

teachings.title: A Platonic gospel of fear
teachings.body: The preacher claims Socrates first proposed, half in jest, that people could be controlled by threatening their non-material part with unprovable punishment, and that Plato adopted it as a tool of social control. The common ‘pray this prayer and avoid punishment after death’ message is called Platonic rather than Jesus’ gospel; he says he is not attacking heaven, hell or judgment.

teachings.title: Jesus and the apostles did not preach it
teachings.body: Jesus and John never preached the fear-based afterlife gospel; Peter is said to have preached it and been corrected. The authentic gospel gives victory in life, not just in death.

teachings.title: Death reigned, but grace reigns in life
teachings.body: Rom 5:13–17: sin is not imputed without law, yet death reigned from Adam to Moses; the free gift is far greater than the offence, and those who receive abundant grace and the gift of righteousness will reign in life through Jesus Christ. This is contrasted with suffering through life to reach a better grave.

teachings.title: Victory visible in every area
teachings.body: The preacher wants a victorious, ever-increasing life seen in his marriage, finances, health and city. The church is a laughingstock when it uses the streets to deliver bad news about post-mortem punishment people did not know they faced.

teachings.title: The gospel lifts decay
teachings.body: The good news is that decay is lifted from one’s life and everything about a person begins to keep pace with an ever-increasing kingdom.

teachings.title: Death means decay, not eternal separation
teachings.body: The series teaches that biblical ‘death’ never denotes torment or eternal separation from God but universal decline and rotting away. He says he is not attacking hell, but ‘fixing your life’.

teachings.title: The ‘over the hill’ expectation
teachings.body: People expect to build until mid-life and then decline — spending down wealth, losing health, skills and relationships — and oddly expect that decay to lead to salvation. If the gospel were about death, the kindest act would be to hold people under longer at baptism.

teachings.title: Question what we take for granted
teachings.body: Western culture rarely questions assumptions; many believe a gospel centred on where they will spend eternity without having read it in the Bible, and try to be soul-winners without realising souls are not the eternal component.

teachings.title: The eternal spirit is secure
teachings.body: Though the soul is not eternal, there is an eternal component of humanity; to be absent from the body is to be eternally present with the Lord. The preacher will not take that away — nor will he rob believers of reigning in life.

teachings.title: Sin and death are the issue, not hell
teachings.body: Rom 5:17 shows the problem is sin and death and the solution righteousness and life. The gospel is not a get-out-of-hell-free pass but a live-abundantly-now, ‘deathless’ pass that removes decay.

teachings.title: Define words by their contexts
teachings.body: The Greek word for human dying is apothnēskō, used repeatedly; the best way to understand a word is to study all its contexts.

teachings.title: Resurrection and the life
teachings.body: At Lazarus’ death Jesus presents Himself as two solutions: the resurrection for those who die (they will live) and the life for those who live and believe (they shall never die). Believers who are alive and believe are therefore ‘deathless’.

teachings.title: Heirs need not die to inherit
teachings.body: Wills and testaments do not require the heir to die to receive the inheritance; so believers need not die to get what is theirs.

teachings.title: Death is a principle of decay
teachings.body: The ultimate end of apothnēskō is the body ceasing, but the full picture of death is decay — anything not keeping pace with an ever-increasing kingdom. Bad moods and anxiety are forms of death.

teachings.title: Jesus’ finances did not decay
teachings.body: At the feeding of the 5,000 Jesus told the disciples to feed the crowd and showed a different economy: what He gave exceeded what He had, and twelve baskets were left. Believers should ask whether death or life reigns in their mood, anxiety, finances, marriage and attitude.

teachings.title: Don’t push promises past the grave
teachings.body: Doctrine that postpones God’s promises to an unseen afterlife keeps believers living as paupers when they should reign now. Only the One who came from the Father has seen Him, so no preacher can prove claims about post-mortem promises; believers should expect and govern increase instead.

teachings.title: Christ shared flesh to destroy death’s power
teachings.body: Because God’s children are flesh and blood, He became human so that through death He might destroy the devil who had the power of death; He let death overtake Him so He could step on its head for us.

teachings.title: Death as an environment of decay
teachings.body: Christ tasted death once for all — meaning not hell or the separation of body and spirit, but the whole environment of decay. Mortal death is the ‘recognition point’ of a life lived under the government of decay.

teachings.title: Bodily death is the recognition, not the event
teachings.body: Like a graduation day recognising years of discipline, bodily death recognises a long period of bondage to death. Being delivered from that bondage is the gospel.

teachings.title: Fear of death causes bondage
teachings.body: Heb 2:15 says Christ releases those who through fear of death were all their lives in bondage. Fear of giving, of relational openness and other anxieties are all fear of decay; once free of the fear of death, a person is free.

teachings.title: Jesus lived free of fear
teachings.body: Jesus could delay four days on hearing Lazarus was sick because He was not a vacuum needing outside supply but the river of life. He gave away loaves and fish knowing His environment was one of increase.

teachings.title: Adam was meant to govern increase
teachings.body: God would not send rain on the garden until Adam was there, because Adam’s responsibility was to govern increase.

teachings.title: Saved means whole now
teachings.body: Sōzō is said to have only natural meanings: healed, delivered, made whole, kept safe and sound, the absence of harm and presence of benefit. Salvation is healing, deliverance, safety, provision and heaven on earth, so a loved one’s salvation should be evident in life, not just in death.

teachings.title: The thief is legalism, not merely the devil
teachings.body: In John 10 the thieves and robbers are those who climb in another way, all who came before Jesus. The series reads them as anyone who teaches that life comes by earning, striving and deserving — legalism is death — whereas Jesus came to give abundant life.

teachings.title: Jesus did not come for post-mortem escape only
teachings.body: John 10:10 does not say Jesus came so we can go to heaven when we die; He tasted death so we would not be stolen from, killed or destroyed, but have abundant life.

teachings.title: Death comes as a seed, received by faith
teachings.body: If your paradigm expects death and decay, you will die in decay ‘by faith’. Sensory triggers around a past tragedy (like a holiday) bring back predictive emotions; that is a seed of death trying to govern you, which you must refuse.

teachings.title: Jesus’ ever-increasing economy
teachings.body: Normal accounting says what I had minus what I gave equals what remains; Jesus’ economy is that one gives much and ends with more. He had no fear of lack, death or disease — touching the leper showed decay had no place in His life.

teachings.title: Key one: choose
teachings.body: Deut 30 says God’s word is near, in mouth and heart, and sets before us life and good, death and evil, urging us to choose life so we and our descendants may live. Every mood, criticism, judgment or offence is a moment to choose life or decay, with grandchildren watching.

teachings.title: Key two: confess
teachings.body: Life and death are in the power of the tongue; every word gives life or kills something, and creation responds to our voice and atmosphere. Having chosen, we must confess what we chose.

teachings.title: Key three: know
teachings.body: God’s people perish for lack of knowledge; believers must be aware and abandon doctrines of death and of demons. People perish because they expect to, not knowing better; a contextual study of apothnēskō is said to show it always means decay, never hell or the grave.

teachings.title: The church is no longer Adamic
teachings.body: Jesus, the last Adam, became like Adam to kill Adam’s shortcomings and rose as the Father’s only begotten Son, placing believers in His death, burial and resurrection. His victory over death is in our past, not our future; today, not death or a repeated prayer, is the day of salvation.

teachings.title: Local churches bring life to regions
teachings.body: God’s design for redeeming creation is the ekklēsia with a government (apostolic outposts) to bring believers to the fullness of Christ so they give life to their metron, their region. Responsibility for the city requires involvement (e.g., addiction recovery) and control of one’s attitude and mood.

teachings.title: A day of repentance from death
teachings.body: No generation has glamorised death more than ours; this is a day to repent of a lifestyle of death and decay. The keys to abundant life are to choose, confess and know.

teachings.title: Physical obedience releases the supernatural
teachings.body: Taking a physical step of obedience brings supernatural release; the congregation extends hands to receive impartation, with expectation that disease and pain will leave, bank accounts be filled and people become supernaturally generous.

stories.title: Tagged out
stories.text: Like a tag-team wrestler, Jesus sat down at the Father’s right hand because He is finished; the powers are defeated and the church is ‘tagged in’ to carry on.

stories.title: Calling back online viewers
stories.text: The preacher addresses local people watching the livestream, excusing international viewers but calling local ones back to the building because the church needs them and life is coming to their town.

stories.title: Socrates’ joke and Plato’s strategy
stories.text: The preacher recounts that Socrates jokingly suggested controlling society by threatening people’s non-material part with punishment, winked at Plato while dying that only his body was being buried, and that Plato then used the idea to manipulate the masses. The point: the afterlife-fear gospel is Platonic, not from Jesus.

stories.title: Street evangelism as bad news
stories.text: A caricature of evangelism — ‘repeat my prayer so you won’t be punished after you die… you didn’t know you’d be punished? So sorry’ — illustrates why the church is mocked: it sacrifices dignity to deliver bad news.

stories.title: Over the hill
stories.text: People spend 55 years earning, learning skills and building health, then expect to spend down, forget and decline to the grave with nothing. Expecting decay to lead to salvation is strange.

stories.title: Holding them under at baptism
stories.text: If the gospel were about death, the most compassionate thing would be to hold people under longer when baptising them — a joke exposing death-centred thinking.

stories.title: Wills and heirs
stories.text: No inheritance requires the heir to die; an heir receives because someone else died. So believers need not die to receive their inheritance.

stories.title: Five loaves and two fish
stories.text: Jesus fed 5,000 with five ordinary loaves and two small fish and had twelve baskets left, showing that in His economy giving does not diminish; His finances did not see decay.

stories.title: Graduation day
stories.text: A diploma ceremony is not the day of success but the recognition of years of discipline. Similarly, bodily death is the recognition of a long life under the bondage of decay.

stories.title: Lazarus and the delay
stories.text: When told Lazarus was sick unto death, Jesus waited days before going. The preacher says He could do so because He was not a vacuum but a life-giving spirit, free from fear.

stories.title: The tragic holiday
stories.text: When someone dies at Christmas, the season’s sights and music trigger grief every year; the preacher calls that predictive emotion a seed of death which people welcome ‘by faith’ unless they know better.

stories.title: Writing a check
stories.text: Ordinary math says balance minus gift equals what’s left; Jesus’ math says give a lot and end with more. Believers are urged to give by Jesus’ economy.

stories.title: Jesus touches the leper
stories.text: Asked if He was willing to cleanse him, Jesus touched the leper, demonstrating that decay and disease had no place in His life.

words.claimed: ‘Monogenetic’ Son: Jesus as uniquely begotten in contrast to Adam, who was merely created and so could not be a son of God.
words.lexicon: BDAG: ‘only, unique, one of a kind’ (from monos + genos, ‘kind’), traditionally ‘only begotten’. It stresses Jesus’ uniqueness, not a genetic process; Luke 3:38 still calls Adam ‘son of God’ in a different sense.

words.claimed: Always means decay — a universal decline; never hell or the grave; its full picture is anything not keeping pace with the kingdom.
words.lexicon: BDAG: to die — of natural physical death; figuratively of spiritual death or dying to sin/the law (Rom 6:2; 7:4; Col 3:3). ‘Decay/corruption’ is a different word family (phthora, diaphthora). The noun thanatos includes ‘the second death’ (Rev 20:14). The claim it always means decay is not supported.

words.claimed: All its definitions are natural: healed, delivered, made whole, kept safe and sound, absence of harm, presence of every benefit.
words.lexicon: BDAG: save, rescue, preserve from harm, heal (Mark 5:34); and very often eschatological salvation from sin, wrath and judgment (Matt 1:21; Rom 5:9; 1 Cor 3:15). Holistic wholeness is a genuine sense, but ‘all definitions are natural’ and ‘presence of all things beneficial’ go beyond the lexicon.

words.claimed: Mind, will and emotions; a non-eternal component that dies with the body.
words.lexicon: BDAG: life, the inner self, the person, seat of feeling and thought; also the self that survives death in some texts (Matt 10:28; Rev 6:9). ‘Mind, will and emotions’ is a popular theological formula, not a lexical definition.

words.claimed: The governing institution meant to govern all of human life.
words.lexicon: BDAG: assembly; in Greek cities a civic assembly of citizens; in the NT the congregation/church. The civic-assembly background supports a governing nuance, though ‘governing all human life’ is an interpretive extension.

words.claimed: A believer’s or church’s assigned region of responsibility.
words.lexicon: BDAG: measure; in 2 Cor 10:13 the measure/sphere (kanōn) God assigned Paul’s ministry.

words.claimed: God rested because He was finished.
words.lexicon: BDB: cease, desist, rest — God ceased from His completed work.

questions.q: Why does the preacher insist believers are not restored to Adam?
questions.a: Adam was created, a living soul and flawed from the start, so restoration to him would bring back his shortcomings. Jesus is the begotten, life-giving Spirit and a new kind of humanity, and believers are placed in Him as the church of the firstborn.

questions.q: What does ‘Deathless’ mean in this part?
questions.a: It means living free from the reign of decay now: through Christ believers reign in life, are freed from fear of death, and — per John 11:26 as read here — those who live and believe ‘shall never die’. Death is understood as any decay not keeping pace with the kingdom.

questions.q: How does the sermon relate the afterlife to the gospel?
questions.a: The afterlife is real — believers are present with the Lord and death has no final say — but it is a component of the gospel, not the gospel. Jesus preached victory on this side of death and never used fear of post-mortem punishment as motivation.

questions.q: What is the significance of Heb 2:14–15 for daily life?
questions.a: Christ destroyed the devil’s power of death and freed people from lifelong bondage to fear of death. Since fears about giving, relationships and loss are forms of fearing decay, freedom from fear of death frees the whole of life.

questions.q: How does the sermon reinterpret the ‘thief’ of John 10:10?
questions.a: The thieves are all who came before Jesus or climb in another way — anyone teaching that life comes by earning, striving and deserving. Legalism is death; Jesus is the door through whom people are saved — made whole — and find abundant life.

questions.q: What are the three keys to life over decay?
questions.a: Choose life (Deut 30), confess life since life and death are in the tongue (Prov 18:21), and know the truth, abandoning doctrines of death, because people perish for lack of knowledge (Hos 4:6).

questions.q: What role does the local church play in this vision?
questions.a: The ekklēsia is God’s governing body to mature believers into Christ’s fullness so they bring life to their region (metron). That requires physical presence, involvement in needs like addiction recovery, and believers governing their own moods and words.

practice: Recommit to active, in-person membership in a local church.
Stop deferring your hope for healing, provision or peace until after death.
Examine areas of your life (mood, anxiety, finances, marriage, attitude) for ‘decay’ and choose life.
Refuse sensory-triggered ‘seeds of death’ such as recurring grief or dread.
Give generously according to Jesus’ economy of increase.
Speak life; watch your words, criticism and complaints.
Study Scripture to replace doctrines of death with knowledge of life.
Reject legalism — earning, striving and deserving — as a route to life.
Model a life of increase for your children and grandchildren.
Get involved in bringing life to your city (e.g., addiction recovery).
Take a physical step of faith and receive prayer for healing.

fair.claim: Believers who live and believe need never physically die (‘deathless’); John 11:26 and Rom 5:17 promise this.
fair.note: Mainstream Christian teaching reads John 11:26 as eternal life that death cannot end — Lazarus himself later died again, as did all the apostles (cf. John 21:18–19 on Peter’s death). Scripture says it is appointed for people to die once (Heb 9:27), the body is dead because of sin (Rom 8:10), and death is the last enemy to be destroyed at Christ’s return (1 Cor 15:26, 51–54). Paul expected his own death and called it gain (Phil 1:21–23; 2 Tim 4:6). Charitable reading: eternal life and victory over the fear and power of death begin now (John 5:24; 8:51), and the series also affirms resurrection and the afterlife.

fair.claim: Jesus never used fear of what happens after death as motivation; the gospel he preached was only about this side of death.
fair.note: Jesus repeatedly warned about judgment after death: fear Him who can destroy soul and body in hell (Matt 10:28; Luke 12:4–5), Gehenna (Mark 9:43–48), the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31), the sheep and goats (Matt 25:46), and the resurrection to judgment (John 5:28–29). Most scholars see Jesus’ kingdom message as both present and future. The charitable point is that Jesus’ gospel was not merely an escape ticket but also present healing, freedom and new life (Luke 4:18–19).

fair.claim: The soul is not an entity; it dies with the body, and only the spirit is eternal.
fair.note: Most Christian traditions hold that the human person (soul/spirit, often used interchangeably) survives death consciously until resurrection: Jesus says the soul cannot be killed by men (Matt 10:28); souls of martyrs speak under the altar (Rev 6:9–10; 20:4). Hebrew nephesh and Greek psychē often mean the whole living person, which some use to support conditional immortality, but even that view does not split a mortal soul from an immortal spirit. ‘Mind, will and emotions’ is a popular formula (tripartite anthropology), not a biblical definition. Charitably, the preacher rightly stresses the whole embodied person and resurrection rather than a disembodied soul.

fair.claim: Socrates jokingly invented the idea of punishment of the soul after death; Plato adopted it to manipulate society, and this is the origin of the church’s gospel.
fair.note: This account is not historical. Belief in the soul’s survival and judgment predates Socrates (Egyptian religion, Orphic and Pythagorean teaching, Homer’s Hades). In Plato’s Phaedo (115c–e) Socrates tells Crito, not Plato, that they bury only his body, and he says it seriously; Plato reports he himself was absent (Phaedo 59b). Plato does discuss useful myths (Republic’s ‘noble lie’, the Myth of Er), but Jewish texts also teach resurrection and judgment (Dan 12:2). Charitably, scholars such as Oscar Cullmann have argued that Platonic ideas of an immortal soul have overshadowed the biblical hope of bodily resurrection — a legitimate critique.

fair.claim: Peter preached the afterlife-fear gospel and ‘got in trouble for it’.
fair.note: No biblical text records Peter being rebuked for preaching about the afterlife. Paul rebuked Peter for withdrawing from Gentile table fellowship (Gal 2:11–14). Peter does speak of judgment of living and dead (Acts 10:42; 1 Pet 4:5) without rebuke.

fair.claim: Biblical ‘death’ never implies eternal separation or torment; apothnēskō always means decay and never hell or the grave.
fair.note: Apothnēskō simply means ‘to die’, overwhelmingly of physical death, and figuratively of dying to sin or the law; ‘decay’ is a different word group (phthora). The NT does speak of ‘the second death’ in the lake of fire (Rev 2:11; 20:14; 21:8), ‘eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord’ (2 Thess 1:9), and spiritual death as alienation from God (Eph 2:1; 4:18). Charitably, death in Scripture is broader than the moment of dying and includes the corruption of creation (Rom 8:21), which the preacher rightly highlights.

fair.claim: Adam was flawed from the beginning and could not be a son of God; Paul contrasts the living soul and life-giving spirit in Romans 5.
fair.note: Genesis calls all creation, including humans, ‘very good’ (Gen 1:31), and Luke 3:38 calls Adam ‘son of God’. Adam was created innocent but mutable; the fall, not the creation, introduced sin (Rom 5:12). The living soul/life-giving spirit contrast is in 1 Cor 15:45, not Romans 5. Charitably, Paul does present Christ as superior to Adam even before the fall — the heavenly man versus the earthly (1 Cor 15:47–49).

fair.claim: Jesus sat down because He is completely finished; the powers are ‘done’ and the church has taken over.
fair.note: Christ’s sacrificial work is finished (Heb 10:12; John 19:30), but Hebrews adds that He waits ‘until His enemies are made a footstool’ (Heb 10:13; Ps 110:1), and Paul says He must reign until all enemies, death last, are destroyed (1 Cor 15:25–26). He also continues to intercede (Heb 7:25). Charitably, the church does share in Christ’s authority and mission (Matt 28:18–20).

fair.claim: Creation waits for the manifestation of the sons, not for Jesus’ coming or a rapture.
fair.note: In Rom 8:19–23 the revealing of the sons is tied to ‘the redemption of our bodies’, i.e., the future resurrection at Christ’s return; Paul links creation’s liberation to that eschatological event (cf. Col 3:4; 1 John 3:2). Views on a ‘rapture’ vary, but most interpreters see the manifestation of the sons and Christ’s appearing as connected rather than opposed. Charitably, believers do now display God’s life as a foretaste.

fair.claim: Sōzō has only natural meanings — wholeness, healing, safety, provision — and salvation is heaven on earth.
fair.note: Sōzō does include healing and rescue (Mark 5:34; Acts 27:20), supporting a holistic view, but it very often refers to salvation from sin, wrath and final judgment (Matt 1:21; Rom 5:9; 1 Cor 3:15; 1 Pet 3:21). Many traditions affirm a holistic salvation that is both present and future.

fair.claim: In John 10 the ‘thief’ is legalism and false teachers, not the devil.
fair.note: This is a well-supported reading: in context the thieves and robbers are false shepherds/leaders who came before Jesus (cf. Ezek 34; John 9:40–41), and many commentators note John 10:10 does not mention the devil. Equating them specifically with any teaching of earning or striving is an application rather than the plain referent, though it fits the Pharisaic context.

fair.claim: Bodily death is the ‘recognition point’ of a life lived under decay; if your paradigm expects death you will die ‘by faith’.
fair.note: This can imply that believers who die (or get sick) did so through wrong belief, which is contrary to texts where the righteous die faithfully (Isa 57:1–2; Acts 7:59–60; Heb 11:13, 39; Rev 14:13) and risks wounding the grieving. Scripture ties universal death to Adam’s sin (Rom 5:12; 1 Cor 15:22), not individual paradigms. Charitably, the preacher urges hope and refusal of fatalism, which Scripture supports.

fair.claim: Jesus’ finances never decayed; giving the Jesus way yields more than you started with, and the closing prayer expects bank accounts to be supernaturally filled.
fair.note: The feeding of the 5,000 is presented in the Gospels as a sign revealing Jesus’ identity (John 6:14, 26–35), not a financial principle; the twelve baskets are not said to be ‘for themselves’. Scripture affirms God’s provision for generous givers (2 Cor 9:6–11; Luke 6:38), but also Jesus’ poverty (Matt 8:20; 2 Cor 8:9) and warnings about wealth (1 Tim 6:5–10). Promises of guaranteed financial increase are associated with prosperity teaching, which many traditions reject.

fair.claim: ‘Life and death are in the power of the tongue’ means every word gives life or kills, and creation responds to our voice.
fair.note: Prov 18:21 is wisdom about the consequences of speech, not a claim that human words govern creation. Words do have real power (Jas 3:5–10), but the idea that creation responds to our voice reflects Word of Faith teaching and is debated. Hos 4:6 refers to the priests’ rejection of knowledge of God and His law.

fair.claim: Heirs never have to die to inherit, so believers need not die to receive their inheritance.
fair.note: Correct about inheritance law, and Heb 9:16–17 supports it: the testator (Christ) died so heirs receive. However, the NT also places much of the inheritance in the future (1 Pet 1:4; Eph 1:14; Col 3:24). Charitably, believers do already possess real blessings in Christ (Eph 1:3).

fair.claim: Minor factual slips: Jesus took a ‘four-day’ delay; God withheld rain until Adam was in the garden.
fair.note: Jesus stayed two more days (John 11:6), and Lazarus had been in the tomb four days on His arrival (John 11:17); the stated reason was God’s glory (John 11:4, 15). Gen 2:5 says there was no rain and no man to work the ground, then a mist watered it; it does not say rain began once Adam was present. These do not affect the main argument.

fair.claim: 1 Pet 1:9’s ‘salvation of your souls’ means the soul coming into harmony with the spirit when no more believing is needed, not eternal destiny.
fair.note: Telos here means outcome or goal; most commentators read 1 Pet 1:3–9 as the final, eschatological salvation ‘ready to be revealed in the last time’ (1:5), i.e., the whole person’s ultimate salvation. The preacher’s soul–spirit harmony reading is idiosyncratic.
